title: Flying Saucer Emoji 🛸 Meaning: UFOs and “Beam Me Up”
description: The 🛸 flying saucer emoji stands for UFOs, aliens and anything out of this world, plus jokes about being abducted from an awkward moment. Examples inside.
summary: 🛸 is a classic disc-shaped UFO. People use it for aliens, sightings and science fiction, for things that feel strange or otherworldly, and for the running joke of wanting to be beamed up and taken away from Earth, work, or an embarrassing situation.
meaning: At face value the flying saucer is about extraterrestrials. News of unexplained aerial sightings, government hearings on the subject, alien movies and conspiracy threads all draw the emoji, usually with the alien face beside it. The saucer shape comes straight from mid-century science fiction, so even serious discussion picks up a slightly retro, tongue-in-cheek flavor when 🛸 appears in it.

Its more common everyday use is escapist humor. “Come get me 🛸” or “abduct me already” is a way of saying a person is done with their surroundings: a boring meeting, bad news, humanity in general. The joke treats aliens as a rescue service. A related use labels someone or something as not of this world, either as a compliment about otherworldly talent or as gentle mockery of odd behavior.

The emoji also belongs to a look. Alien and space imagery has been a recurring style in fashion, rave culture and online aesthetics, and 🛸 shows up in usernames, bios and captions alongside planets, stars and green hearts simply because it fits the palette. Added in 2017, it arrived when many of those trends were already under way and was adopted quickly.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: Friends send 🛸 to say something was bizarre (“that date was 🛸”) or to wish themselves elsewhere. It works as a reply to weird news in place of typing “what planet is this.” Because the tone is playful, it softens a complaint; asking to be abducted is funnier than saying you are miserable.

contexts.label: On TikTok and Instagram
contexts.body: Creators use the saucer on videos of strange lights in the sky, desert road trips near Roswell or Area 51, and alien-themed makeup and outfits. In comments, a row of saucers can mean the content is out of this world, or that the commenter thinks the poster is living on another planet.

contexts.label: In fandoms and pop culture
contexts.body: Science fiction fans attach 🛸 to posts about series and films involving alien visitors, and musicians with space-themed releases use it in rollout posts. Around Halloween it helps announce alien costumes. Sports and gaming communities borrow it to call a performance unreal, meaning beyond normal human ability.

examples.text: If any aliens are reading this, come get me 🛸
examples.meaning: A joke about wanting to escape a tiring day or situation.

examples.text: Saw three lights hovering over the lake last night 🛸👀
examples.meaning: Reporting a possible UFO sighting, half serious and half amused.

examples.text: Her vocals on that track are 🛸
examples.meaning: Praise: the performance is so good it seems from another world.
A travel caption from the New Mexico town famous for UFO lore.
Teasing someone for behavior the sender finds strange.

combos.meaning: Aliens and their ship; the standard pairing for UFO talk and extraterrestrial jokes.
A cow being abducted, referencing a long-running trope in UFO stories and cartoons.
Waiting to be picked up by aliens; used to say “take me away from here.”
A spacey, dreamy aesthetic used in captions and usernames.

confusedWith.difference: 🚀 is a human spacecraft and mostly signals launches, growth and ambition. 🛸 is an alien vehicle tied to mystery, weirdness and jokes about leaving the planet.
👽 is the passenger rather than the craft. It can describe a person feeling like an outsider, whereas 🛸 points to sightings, abduction jokes and arrival from elsewhere.
👾 is a pixelated arcade creature linked to video games. It has little to do with UFO culture, despite sharing the word alien in its name.

avoid: Avoid using it to call a person weird if they might take it as an insult rather than a joke.
Leave it off serious scientific or defense reporting unless a lighter tone is intended, because it frames the topic as kitsch.
design: The emoji shows a metallic disc with a domed cockpit on top, the saucer of 1950s film posters. Most versions are gray or silver with a ring of lights around the rim, and some designs add a beam of light shining down from the underside, as if lifting something aboard. The dome may be clear, blue or green depending on the platform.

faqs.a: It most often means strange or out of this world. It can praise something as unreal, tease someone as spacey, or express a wish to be carried off somewhere else.

faqs.q: When did the flying saucer emoji come out?
faqs.a: It was added in 2017 as part of Emoji 5.0, the same release that introduced other fantasy and science fiction characters to the keyboard.

faqs.q: What does 🛸 mean from a guy or a girl?
faqs.a: There is no flirting code attached to it. Depending on the sentence it either jokes about escape, comments that something is weird, or signals interest in aliens and space.
It is the emoji people use for UFOs, though strictly a UFO is any unidentified object. The emoji depicts one specific pop-culture idea of it: the round alien saucer.
